Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key findings: First episode of sudden-onset unilateral (left) headache with visual disturbance (blurred vision with zigzag lines), nausea/vomiting, dizziness, and photophobia. No focal neurological deficits reported on history; gait normal. Family history of migraine. Acetaminophen ineffective.
- Differential diagnoses (consistent with DDx):
  - Migraine with visual aura: Highly consistent with unilateral pain, visual aura, nausea/vomiting, photophobia, and family history. 
  - Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH): Less likely but considered due to first sudden severe headache and vomiting at onset; absence of neurologic deficits and “worst-ever” description reduces likelihood; no exam/vitals available.
  - Cervical artery dissection: Low likelihood; unilateral acute headache and dizziness without neck pain/trauma or focal deficits.
- Working diagnosis: Migraine with visual aura.
- Management priorities: Symptom relief; timely in-person neurological examination to exclude secondary causes given first, sudden-onset headache with vomiting; safety-netting for any deterioration or new neurologic symptoms.

Management Plan

- Actions and recommendations:
  - Trial ibuprofen plus an OTC antiemetic (from pharmacy); drink a sugary carbonated beverage (e.g., Coke). Dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Same-day in-person appointment arranged for neurological assessment; if markedly improved before appointment, patient may cancel per clinician advice.
  - Safety net: Contact clinic if symptoms worsen or new neurological symptoms occur before the appointment.
  - If inadequate response, consider escalation to specific migraine therapies as discussed with clinician.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):

- Migraine with visual aura – Likelihood: High. Justification: Unilateral headache, visual zigzag lines, photophobia, nausea/vomiting, family history, no focal deficits.
- Subarachnoid hemorrhage (aneurysmal SAH) – Likelihood: Moderate. Justification: First, sudden-onset headache with vomiting at onset; lack of exam/vitals leaves residual concern.
- Cervical artery dissection – Likelihood: Low. Justification: Unilateral acute headache and dizziness; no neck pain/trauma or focal neurological signs.
